Yes, ...","url":"https://clinekthealth.com/blog/do-appointment-reminders-reduce-no-shows"}]

Here's what the evidence shows on no-show rates, scheduling software, and reminders:

## The core finding: reminders help, but modestly

Controlled studies show automated reminders cut no-shows by a weighted mean of 28.9%, and staff phone calls by 39.1%, relative to no reminder (Hasvold & Wootton, 2011). In one widely cited study, non-attendance fell from 18.1% to 11.2% with SMS reminders — a 38% relative reduction (Koshy, Car & Majeed, 2008).

An important caveat: reminders only address one cause of missed appointments — forgetting — which is why studies still show a meaningful residual no-show rate even after reminders are in place. No study arm gets no-shows anywhere near zero.

## Automated vs. human reminders

Human contact consistently outperforms automation. A prospective randomized study of 13,505 appointments demonstrated a lower no-show rate with a clinic staff reminder compared with an automated appointment reminder, leading the authors to conclude that outpatient automated reminder systems are less effective in reducing no-show rates compared with receiving a reminder from live clinic staff. A three-arm study found live staff calls produced a 13.6% no-show rate versus 17.3% for automated reminders (Parikh et al., 2010).

Not all research agrees reminders work at all: Hixon and colleagues found no difference in no-show rates when clinics used reminder systems.

## Volunteer-specific claims (treat cautiously)

Most vendor and guide content extrapolates from healthcare research rather than citing volunteer-sector studies:

- One source claims a study by Molfenter in *Substance Use & Misuse* examined 67 treatment organizations implementing the STAR-SI program between 2007 and 2010, finding automated reminders combined with process improvements reduced appointment no-show rates from 37.4% to 19.9% — note this is a healthcare appointment study, not volunteering, and reminders were bundled with process improvements.
- A practitioner guide estimates that no-show rates typically drop from 20–30% to 10–15% with automatic reminders, with reminders sent 24–48 hours before a shift reducing no-shows by 30–40%. These figures appear to be practitioner estimates rather than published findings.

## Related design factor: self-scheduling

In a 2025 study, appointments booked online at a private medical practice had a 1.8% no-show rate versus 5.9% for offline bookings. This suggests self-service signup — a standard feature in volunteer platforms — may matter independently of reminders, though selection effects likely inflate the gap.

## Bottom line

There is no robust peer-reviewed literature on *volunteer* no-shows specifically; the credible numbers all come from healthcare appointment research. Expect roughly a 25–40% relative reduction from automated reminders, with personal contact outperforming automation, and don't expect reminders to solve no-shows caused by illness, transport, or genuine conflicts — issues not addressed by reminders, such as poor weather, sickness, and transportation, were each cited by fewer than 8% of patients in one VHA analysis.

Links: [{"title":"The Effectiveness of Text Message Reminders on Improving ...","url":"https://hsrc.himmelfarb.gwu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1208&context=son_dnp"},{"title":"Pragmatic Randomized Study of Targeted Text Message Reminders to Reduce Missed Clinic Visits","url":"https://www.thepermanentejournal.org/doi/10.7812/TPP/21.078"},{"title":"Pragmatic Randomized Study of Targeted Text Message Reminders to Reduce Missed Clinic Visits - PubMed","url":"https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35609163/"},{"title":"Text Message Reminders Increase Appointment Adherence in a Pediatric Clinic: A Randomized Controlled Trial","url":"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5227159/"},{"title":"Text Message Reminders Increase Appointment Adherence in a Pediatric Clinic: A Randomized Controlled Trial - PubMed","url":"https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28127311"},{"title":"Text-messaging versus telephone reminders to reduce missed appointments in an academic primary care clinic: a randomized controlled trial","url":"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3623700/"},{"title":"Stating Appointment Costs in SMS Reminders Reduces Missed Hospital Appointments: Findings from Two Randomised Controlled Trials","url":"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4569397/"},{"title":"SMS Appointment Reminders Reduce No-Show Rate: Study","url":"https://notifyre.com/us/blog/appointment-reminders-statistiscs"},{"title":"Walden University Walden University ScholarWorks ScholarWorks","url":"https://scholarworks.waldenu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=21191&context=dissertations"},{"title":"Optimizing Number and Timing of Appointment Reminders: A Randomized Trial","url":"https://www.ajmc.com/view/optimizing-number-and-timing-of-appointment-reminders-a-randomized-trial"}]

Here's what the research literature shows on text message reminders and attendance/no-show reduction:

## Core randomized trial evidence

**Pediatric clinic RCT** — A randomized controlled trial tested text reminders on attendance adherence at a pediatric resident clinic serving an inner-city population, with patients randomized 1:1 to receive a text or not, in addition to the standard clinic phone message. The no-show rate was significantly lower in the intervention group (23.5%) than the control group (38.1%), a difference of 14.6% (p = 0.04). No demographic factors altered the association between no-show rate and the text message intervention.

**Text vs. telephone (non-inferiority)** — A randomized controlled non-inferiority trial at Geneva University Hospitals' primary care division randomly assigned patients to receive either a text message or a telephone call reminder one day before the appointment. Text-message reminders were found equivalent to telephone reminders in reducing missed appointments, and more cost-effective.

## Optimizing number and timing

**Three-armed trial** — Two reminders delivered by text message or telephone 3 days and 1 day prior to a primary care visit were more effective than a single reminder delivered either 3 days or 1 day prior. The benefit was particularly pronounced in patients whom a clinical prediction rule identified as at high risk of missing appointments.

**Risk-targeted reminders (Kaiser Permanente Washington)** — Because sending multiple reminders for every visit is costly, risk prediction models can be used to target reminders for visits likely to be missed. This pragmatic randomized quality improvement project compared one text reminder (2 business days prior) with two reminders (2 and 3 days prior) among high no-show-risk primary care and mental health visits, randomizing 125,076 primary care and 33,593 mental health visits between February and September 2019, using G-computation with logistic regression adjusted for no-show risk. The authors concluded that using a prediction model to target reminders may reduce no-shows and allocate resources more efficiently.

## Message content/framing (relevant for volunteer recruitment messaging)

Two UK randomised controlled trials enrolled outpatients with valid mobile numbers — 10,111 participants in Trial One and 9,848 in Trial Two. In Trial One, a message stating the cost of a missed appointment to the health system produced a "Did Not Attend" rate of 8.4% versus 11.1% for the existing message (OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.61–0.89, P<0.01). A separate arm tested a "social norms" message communicating that attending was the dominant norm.

## Synthesis / meta-analytic evidence

A Cochrane systematic review pooling seven randomized trials (5,841 participants) found mobile text message reminders improved appointment attendance compared to no reminders (risk ratio 1.14, 95% CI 1.03–1.26), though the evidence quality was rated low to moderate. The same review found text reminders performed about as well as phone calls, but at lower cost per completed appointment.

A caveat worth noting: nearly all of this evidence comes from **clinical appointment** settings rather than research volunteer/study-visit attendance specifically. If your interest is research participant retention, the design principles (two reminders at ~72h and ~24h, risk-targeting, cost/norm framing) transfer plausibly, but you may want a dedicated search on clinical trial visit adherence or research participant retention RCTs. Links: [{"title":"The Art of Volunteer Retention: How Volunteer Management Software Creates a Thriving Culture","url":"https://www.vomevolunteer.com/blog/the-art-of-volunteer-retention-how-volunteer-management-software-creates-a-thriving-culture"},{"title":"Optimization of volunteer task assignments to improve volunteer retention and nonprofit organizational performance - ScienceDirect","url":"https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0038012122001872"},{"title":"A Low-Cost Way to Improve Volunteer Retention","url":"https://carlsonschool.umn.edu/news/low-cost-way-improve-volunteer-retention"},{"title":"The 16 Top Volunteer Management Tools for Nonprofits in 2026 - Neon One","url":"https://neonone.com/resources/blog/volunteer-management-software/"},{"title":"10 Best Volunteer Management Software for Nonprofits (2025)","url":"https://onlinedegrees.sandiego.edu/volunteer-management-software/"},{"title":"AI for Volunteer Management: Matching, Scheduling, Retention","url":"https://scottshipsolutions.com/blog/ai-nonprofits-volunteer-management/"},{"title":"Keep 33% More New Volunteers with Automation [Guide]","url":"https://ustechautomations.com/resources/blog/nonprofit-volunteer-management-automation-pain-solution-2026"},{"title":"Best Nonprofit Volunteer Management Automation Tools Compared 2026","url":"https://ustechautomations.com/resources/blog/nonprofit-volunteer-management-automation-comparison"},{"title":"Nonprofit Volunteer Management Automation: How to Cut ...","url":"https://ustechautomations.com/resources/blog/nonprofit-volunteer-management-automation-how-to-2026"},{"title":"How to Keep Volunteers Coming Back After Their First Shift - Management.org","url":"https://management.org/how-to-keep-volunteers-coming-back-after-their-first-shift"}]

Here's what the search turned up, organized by type of source:

## Peer-reviewed / academic research

**Shift composition and retention (the strongest empirical finding)**A study published in *Manufacturing & Service Operations Management*, using five years of data from 49,378 volunteers at a food bank, found that simply having an experienced volunteer present on a shift increases new-volunteer retention by 52%. The effect was reported as a 52% retention lift for solo volunteers and a 125% lift for group volunteers.

This appears to be the same work covered by the University of Minnesota Carlson School: Supply Chain & Operations Assistant Professor Vinit Tipnis' paper "Enhancing Volunteer Retention: The Role of Experienced Volunteers" shows how pairing experienced, longtime volunteers with newcomers can improve retention. Tipnis analyzed five years of volunteer data from Gleaners Food Bank of Indiana and found that when an experienced volunteer worked a shift with new volunteers, the new volunteers were more likely to return. Notably, there's a nonlinearity: having several experienced volunteers who all know each other on the same shift negates the benefits — and actually reduces retention among new volunteers. The practical implication is scheduling-driven rather than tech-driven: nonprofits can use "soft scheduling" of shifts to improve retention at no cost.

**Optimization / OR literature**
A *Socio-Economic Planning Sciences* paper takes a scheduling-as-optimization angle: it develops an integer program to generate volunteer and employee task assignments over a program planning horizon, capturing volunteer retention considerations alongside organizational and task-urgency needs. A key constraint is that although volunteer labor is free, volunteers must be trained before assignment, and nonprofit employees' time is limited. Relevant to your "technology shift" framing: the paper notes that nonprofits have adopted online scheduling platforms that give volunteers autonomy in the scheduling process.

Also referenced: the *Journal of Public and Nonprofit Affairs* found that opportunities for skill development and advancement significantly increase retention rates.

## Practitioner / industry sources (treat figures cautiously — mostly vendor-published)

These results are dominated by software-vendor and consultancy blogs, so the statistics are not peer-reviewed and often lack methodology:

- Nonprofit Tech for Good's 2025 Global NGO Technology Survey is cited for organizations implementing volunteer management automation reducing coordination time by 50–65% while increasing retention by 28%.
- AFP Global research is cited for retention improvements of 25–40% among nonprofits implementing structured volunteer management systems versus informal coordination.
- Urban Institute research is cited for retention rates 20–30% higher at nonprofits with comprehensive volunteer management practices.
- Reliability/no-show angle: VolunteerHub's retention research is cited for 58% of non-returning volunteers citing "lack of communication between shifts." Better Impact is cited for 6-month retention of 78% where post-shift appreciation plus monthly impact updates are used, versus 52% with no between-shift communication.
- Baseline tooling gap: spreadsheet-based scheduling is reported as the most common coordination method at mid-size nonprofits — 52% of organizations with 200+ volunteers.
- A useful caveat from the same body of writing: the organizations with the highest retention are described not as those with the most sophisticated technology, but those whose coordinators spend the most time with volunteers rather than spreadsheets.

## Assessment for research purposes

If you need genuinely academic sources, the two to pursue are the *M&SOM* experienced-volunteer paper (Tipnis) and the integer-programming assignment literature in *Socio-Economic Planning Sciences*. The broader "does volunteer management software improve retention and shift reliability" question is thinly covered in peer-reviewed work — most quantified claims trace back to vendor benchmark reports rather than independent studies. Would you like me to search specifically for journal literature (e.g., *Nonprofit and Voluntary Sector Quarterly*, *VOLUNTAS*) on ICT adoption and volunteer reliability/no-show behavior?
